newsitem.title: ITALY: Employers attack Italy govt, OECD more supportive.
newsitem.headline: Employers attack Italy govt, OECD more supportive.

text.p: Italian industrialists warned on Wednesday that Italy risked missing the launch of the single European currency but the OECD said tough government budget action might do the trick.

Giorgio Fossa, the head of employers' organisation Confindustria, said in a hard-hitting speech that Prime Minister Romano Prodi's seven month old administration risked being "blown away" unless it changed its policies.
"Like all buildings constructed on sand, even the bricks of this, as of any other government, risk being blown away in the first gale," Fossa said.

However Prodi received a boost from the Paris-based Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), which said Italy might meet a key requirement laid out in the Maastricht Treaty for states wishing to join the euro currency.

In an upbeat report released ahead of time on Wednesday, the OECD said Italy might succeed in cutting its public sector deficit to three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) in 1997 thanks to tough government budget plans for next year.
Confindustria denied this, saying fresh financial measures would be needed next year if Prodi was to tame the deficit.

"On the deficit/GDP ratio, the uncertainty is not over if Italy will reach the three percent target but over how much it will overshoot," Confindustria's chief economist Giampaolo Galli said, predicting a ratio of 4.8 percent.
Under the terms of the Maastricht Treaty, founder countries of the new euro, which is due to be launched in 1999, must have a deficit/GDP ratio of three percent.

Prodi's office immediately sent a statement highlighting the OECD report, which was not meant to be published until next week. "The government just wants to say that international institutions like the OECD...differ strongly from Confindustria's pessimistic outlook," it said.

However the OECD report, prepared some weeks ago, was based on the premise that this year's deficit would be around 124 trillion lire ($81.4 billion). Latest unofficial estimates say it will be closer to 140 trillion lire.

"What will happen when the markets discover that the budget will not guarantee the three percent ratio between deficit and GDP, that the 1997 deficit will be higher than expected and that pensions spending remains out of control?" Fossa said.

The employers' body also predicted economic growth much lower than the government's two percent forecast for 1997 -- a forecast echoed by the OECD which said Italian GDP would increase by just 1.2 percent next year.

Confindustria has clashed regularly with the government over its 1997 budget, which is designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire off next year's projected deficit through a mix of tax increases, spending cuts and treasury operations.
Fossa has argued that too much emphasis has been put on tax hikes and not enough on structural spending cuts.
The upper house of parliament is currently examining the budget and has until December 19 to approve the bill.
Former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi pledged late on Tuesday that the centre-right opposition would continue its parliamentary protest over the deficit-cutting package.
A senior politician from the governing coalition said on Wednesday that Prodi might call a confidence vote to sweep aside nearly 3,500 amendments to the budget bill.
